title: Vikas Khanna Says Indian Food Abroad Is Still Taking Baby Steps
excerpt: Nearly 27 years into his career, the Michelin-starred chef behind New York's Bungalow talks to Indulge Express about regional dishes, daily consistency, and why Indian cuisine needs no Western validation certificate.
body:
• Michelin-starred chef Vikas Khanna, nearly 27 years into his career, says Indian food abroad is still taking "baby steps" beyond butter chicken — every travelling cuisine is first known by a smaller set of dishes than it really has.
  • At Bungalow in New York, now running for over two years, his answer is regional breadth: he cites a gongura dish for a Telangana celebration and a chilli pickle from Jharkhand served recently.
  • Khanna says Bungalow can have 10,000 people on its waiting list, and that the experience starts long before the meal — families try for reservations at 11 a.m. and then wait about 20 days.
  • His rule for staying authentic: show up in the kitchen every day, do not chase fads on social media, and do not seek a Western "validation certificate" for Indian food.

Vikas Khanna has spent nearly 27 years cooking, and he is still in his own kitchen every day. In an interview with Indulge Express ahead of Deepavali, the Michelin-starred chef described where Indian food abroad actually stands: not transformed, but learning its alphabet.

"I feel it's a baby step," Khanna said, asked how perception has changed beyond butter chicken after more than two years of running Bungalow in New York. "Italians can say the same thing: they're not only about pizza and pasta, they are more than that. Thai people can say we are more than pad Thai and green and red curries, right? Every cuisine, which travels abroad, has a perception that is generally smaller than what the cuisine is. It's a baby step. We learn how to write the alphabet, then the words and the stories. I feel it is very important to not rush it."

Consistency, and a new dish every week

Khanna said he has not been "overwhelmed by television and reality shows" and does not leave the kitchen. The commitment, he said, is to what should appeal to guests — "not just consistency of the food, the service and the values, but also innovation." Bungalow, he said, can create a dish every week and put it out, "a dish the world has never seen before," connecting not just with Indians but with the Western world.

https://www.instagram.com/reel/Dfc1A_qGQbT/

That regional expansion is concrete on the menu. Khanna told Indulge Express the restaurant recently served an entire dish of gongura when celebrating Telangana — a flavour many diners did not know was part of Indian food — and a dish with a chilli pickle from Jharkhand that "people went crazy for." His most popular dish, he said, is pineapple curry — a dish he noted Indian parents would not walk into a restaurant and order, which for him proves that diners will try something new when it is done with confidence. His one indispensable ingredient, he said, is ghee: "I'm very obsessed with ghee."

"Our goal is to try to expand the standard, the idea of India, every day."

— Vikas Khanna, to Indulge Express

The same argument, in his other interviews

The Indulge Express conversation matches what Khanna has said elsewhere about how he built Bungalow's menu. In an interview with Variety India, he explained that Indian food abroad gained its first engagement through Butter Chicken, Dal Makhani, Naan and Garlic Naan — and that, with that engagement secured, he kept only three Punjabi dishes on the menu and added dishes from Odisha and Bengal, condiments from Pondicherry, and spices from Gujarat, Rajasthan and Kashmir. "The menu embodies the entire spirit of India," he said.

On the line between innovation and dilution, his answer in that interview was direct: his competition is not other New York restaurants, but "the chefs and restaurants that are cooking Indian food in India, food in Indian homes, and [food cooked] by street vendors." Authenticity, in that framing, is the benchmark the innovation has to meet.

Authenticity over trends

Khanna told Indulge Express that the meal at Bungalow is meant to feel like "going on a summer holiday to your grandma's house" — a homecoming, not something superficial. "We have to show ourselves as we are, our most authentic selves," he said, adding that even in an age when AI can create perfect videos, people still relate to something authentic.

The same choice shapes his online presence. He said it was a conscious decision not to fall into "a category called a fad," that he does not do tabletop cooking, and that Bungalow was launched through Instagram, speaking directly to the audience, without a PR company. He has also been appointed a judge for Instagram Rings this year, he noted — an honour he described in terms of community, not reach.

And success, for him, no longer needs outside approval. "It is so sacred to me that it doesn't require the Western world to give you a validation certificate saying that, yes, you can eat at Bungalow," he said.

What this means for diaspora diners

For Indian American readers, Khanna's "baby steps" framing is useful expectation-setting: the wider menu — gongura, regional pickles, dishes beyond the Punjabi canon — is arriving restaurant by restaurant, led by chefs willing to put unfamiliar regional dishes in front of diners who came in for butter chicken. At Bungalow itself, plan well ahead: Khanna described families getting on different computers at 11 o'clock to try for a reservation, followed by about 20 days of waiting before the visit.
nri_angle: Khanna's Bungalow in New York is expanding what diaspora and Western diners expect from Indian food, one regional dish at a time.
author: Diaspora Desk
